concepts.def: Deterrence, retribution, reformation, protection, reparation; Christianity emphasises reformation; modern justice mixes aims.
Death penalty; Christians divided (Catholics now oppose); Sharia permits for murder; abolished in UK 1965.
Victim-offender dialogue and reparation; mirrors Christian forgiveness and Jewish teshuvah (return).
Offences motivated by prejudice against identity; Sentencing Act 2020 enhanced penalties; religions condemn.
'Eye for an eye' (Exodus 21:24); originally limited excessive revenge; Jesus reinterpreted (Matthew 5:38).
Christianity Matthew 18:22 'seventy times seven'; Islam Qur'an 24:22; central to dealing with crime.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Capital punishment = death penalty for serious crime.

Abolished in the UK in 1965 (full abolition 1998). Still legal in some US states, China, Iran, Saudi Arabia.

Arguments for: deterrence, retribution ('eye for an eye'), protects society. Arguments against: sanctity of life, irreversible if wrong, no clear deterrent effect, expensive.

Christianity is divided.

Against: Pope Francis declared capital punishment 'inadmissible' (2018, Catechism update). Jesus stopped the stoning of the adulteress (John 8). Sanctity of life — only God should take life.

For: some Christians point to Genesis 9:6 ('whoever sheds human blood, by humans shall their blood be shed') and Romans 13 — the state has the sword. But this view is now a minority.

Islam allows capital punishment for certain serious crimes — murder, treason, apostasy in some interpretations.

However, the Qur'an strongly encourages mercy and forgiveness: Surah 5:32 condemns unjust killing.

In practice, victims' families may accept compensation (diyya) instead. Many Muslim countries have moved away from regular executions; some retain the death penalty in shari'ah law.
